summary.text: The lipid bilayer is a thin polar membrane made of two layers of lipid molecules that forms a continuous barrier around all cells.
It keeps ions, proteins and other molecules where they are needed, because it is impermeable to most water-soluble molecules.
When phospholipids are exposed to water they self-assemble into a two-layered sheet, with their hydrophobic tails pointing toward the center.

facts.label: Core thickness
facts.value: The hydrophobic core is typically 3-4 nm thick

facts.label: Main building block
facts.value: Phospholipids with a hydrophilic head and a hydrophobic tail

facts.label: Cholesterol's role
facts.value: Strengthens the bilayer and decreases permeability in animal cells

facts.label: How it is studied
facts.value: Electron microscopy and atomic force microscopy

items.prompt: A cell needs more salt inside than outside. How does it manage this given its membrane?

options.label: Bilayers block ions, so ion pumps move them across
Bilayers let salt pass freely, so the water around pushes it in
Ion pumps are lipids that dissolve a gap in the bilayer
The bilayer tails soak up salt and release it inside

items.explain: Bilayers are particularly impermeable to ions, so cells regulate salt concentrations by moving ions across with proteins called ion pumps.

items.prompt: Phospholipids are dropped into a watery solution. What arrangement do they self-assemble into?

options.label: A single flat layer, with the tails pointing to the water
A two-layered sheet, with the tails pointing to the water
A two-layered sheet, with the tails pointing to the center
A random mix, spread evenly through the solution

items.explain: When exposed to water, phospholipids form a two-layered sheet with the hydrophobic tails pointing toward the center.

items.prompt: A model bilayer is cooled down in a lab. What can happen to it?

options.label: It can become a looser, runnier fluid
It can settle into a solid gel phase
It can dissolve into the surrounding water
It can flip so the tails face outward

items.explain: The bilayer can adopt a solid gel phase at lower temperatures and become fluid at higher temperatures.

items.prompt: An animal cell needs a stronger membrane that is less leaky. What helps?

options.label: More fusion proteins joining bilayers together
A thinner layer of heads on each side
Extra ion pumps working across the sheet
Cholesterol in the bilayer

items.explain: In animal cells, cholesterol helps strengthen the bilayer and decrease its permeability.

items.prompt: Why are lipid bilayers difficult to study?

options.label: They are fragile and invisible in a traditional microscope
They are too thick for any light to pass
They fall apart whenever they are made in a lab
They exist only inside living cells

items.explain: Because bilayers are fragile and invisible in a traditional microscope they are hard to study, and model bilayers can be made in a lab.

items.prompt: A sperm reaches an egg, and their two membranes must merge. What helps this fusion happen?

options.label: Cholesterol packing the two leaflets tightly
Ion pumps moving salt across the barrier
Certain kinds of membrane proteins
The bilayers dissolving into the water first

items.explain: Certain kinds of membrane proteins are involved in fusing two bilayers together, as in fertilization of an egg by a sperm.
